## What this exercise is

Exercises 1--3 ran on data that shipped inside an R package. This one
does not. You will work with **real surveillance data** --- COVID-19
deaths in the 67 counties of Pennsylvania --- and assemble the analysis
dataset yourself, the way you would in a health department: a table of
counts from one source, county boundaries from another, and a join
between them that has to be checked rather than trusted.

From there the exercise follows the sequence of the last two weeks:

1.  join and project the data;
2.  compute crude rates, **expected counts**, and the **standardized
    mortality ratio (SMR)**;
3.  map the SMR honestly --- which, for a ratio, is not the same as
    mapping a rate;
4.  build a spatial weights matrix and ask, with **global Moran's I**,
    whether the SMRs are spatially structured or could plausibly be
    arranged at random.

It is worth 17.5 points and carries more weight than the first two
exercises. Start early: Part A is where most of the unexpected problems
will be.

## The data

**Counts.** `pa_covid_deaths_2020.csv` is posted on Course Site. It is a
subset of the **Johns Hopkins University CSSE COVID-19 Data Repository**
(`time_series_covid19_deaths_US.csv`), the source behind the JHU
dashboard that was the most widely used COVID-19 tracker in the United
States until the project stopped updating in March 2023. The repository
compiles counts reported by state health departments --- here, the
Pennsylvania Department of Health --- and attributes deaths to the
county of residence.

| Column | Meaning |
|------------------------------------|------------------------------------|
| `UID`, `FIPS` | JHU identifier; county FIPS code |
| `Admin2` | County name |
| `Province_State` | State |
| `Population` | County population (U.S. Census Bureau 2019 estimate, as carried in the JHU file) |
| `deaths_2020` | Cumulative COVID-19 deaths reported through December 31, 2020 |

Cite the source in your document as: Dong, E., Du, H., & Gardner, L.
(2020). An interactive web-based dashboard to track COVID-19 in real
time. *The Lancet Infectious Diseases, 20*(5), 533--534, together with
the repository URL: <https://github.com/CSSEGISandData/COVID-19>.

**Boundaries.** County polygons come from the U.S. Census Bureau's
**cartographic boundary files**, downloaded inside your document with
the `tigris` package. Install it once, in the console ---
`install.packages(c("tigris", "ggrepel"))` --- not inside the document.

::: callout-note
## Why 2020

Calendar year 2020 is the first pandemic year and the period before
vaccines were available. Treat the population as the population at risk
for one year.
:::

```{r}
#| label: setup

library(sf)
library(dplyr)
library(readr)
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)
library(leaflet)
library(spdep)
library(ggrepel)            # non-overlapping labels
library(tigris)
options(tigris_use_cache = TRUE)   # download once, then reuse

covid <- read_csv("data/pa_covid_deaths_2020.csv")
pa    <- counties(state = "PA", cb = TRUE, year = 2020)
```

## Part A --- Assemble the dataset (3 points)

1.  Inspect both objects. How many rows does `covid` have, and how many
    polygons does `pa` have? The two numbers differ. Find the rows
    responsible and say in one sentence what they are and why they
    cannot be mapped.
2.  Identify the column in each object that identifies a county. Show
    what the values look like in each, and say why they will not match
    as they stand.
3.  Create a join key in `covid` that matches the one in `pa`, then
    **join the counts onto the polygons**. Show, with code, that every
    one of the 67 counties received a count --- do not just look at the
    map.
4.  In two or three sentences: why join the table onto the polygons
    (`left_join(pa, covid)`) rather than the other way around, and what
    would an **inner** join have hidden from you if the key had been
    only partly wrong?

::: callout-tip
Run the obvious join first,
`left_join(pa, covid, by = c("GEOID" = "FIPS"))`, and read the error
message carefully. It tells you exactly what is wrong. A FIPS code is an
**identifier**, not a number: `42001` and `42001.0` are the same number
but not the same identifier, and a county such as `01001` in Alabama
would lose its leading zero.
:::

### Starting code

```{r}
#| label: a-starter

# A1
covid
pa
nrow(covid); nrow(pa)

# Rows in the table with no matching polygon
anti_join(
  covid,
  st_drop_geometry(pa),
  by = c("Admin2" = "NAME")
)

# A2 -- what type is each key?
str(covid$FIPS)
str(pa$GEOID)

# Show example values
head(covid$FIPS)
head(pa$GEOID)

# A3 -- a five-character, zero-padded text key
covid <- covid |>
  mutate(GEOID = sprintf("%05d", as.integer(FIPS)))
# Join the counts onto the county polygons
pa_covid <- pa |>
  left_join(covid, by = "GEOID")

# Verify that all 67 counties received a count
nrow(pa_covid)
sum(is.na(pa_covid$deaths_2020))
sum(!is.na(pa_covid$deaths_2020))

# Stop execution if the verification fails
stopifnot(
  nrow(pa_covid) == 67,
  n_distinct(pa_covid$GEOID) == 67,
  !anyNA(pa_covid$deaths_2020)
)
```

Answers:

1)  covid has 69 rows, and pa has 67 county polygons. The two extra
    rows, “Out of PA” and “Unassigned,” cannot be mapped because neither
    identifies a specific Pennsylvania county.

2)  The county code is stored in FIPS in covid and GEOID in pa. FIPS
    contains numbers such as 42001, while GEOID contains text such as
    "42033". They cannot be joined directly because one column is
    numeric and the other is text.

3)  I converted the FIPS codes into five-character text codes called
    GEOID and used them to join the counts onto the county polygons. The
    joined dataset has 67 counties and no missing death counts,
    confirming that every county received a count.

4)  Using left_join(pa, covid) keeps the county polygons as the main
    dataset, so all 67 counties remain available for mapping even if
    some counts fail to match. If a join key were wrong for a county,
    that county would remain with a missing count, making the problem
    visible. An inner join would silently remove that county, hiding the
    failed match and leaving an incomplete map.

## Part B --- Coordinate reference system (1.5 points)

1.  What CRS do the Census boundaries arrive in? Geographic or
    projected?
2.  Transform `pa_covid` to a **projected** CRS appropriate for the
    whole state, and state its EPSG code. Pennsylvania is split between
    two State Plane zones (North and South) and two UTM zones, so the
    obvious choices each cover only part of the state --- say what you
    chose and why it is acceptable for a statewide map.
3.  One sentence: which of the operations in this exercise actually
    depend on the projection, and which do not?

### Starting code

```{r}
#| label: b-starter

# Check the original CRS
st_crs(pa_covid)$input
st_is_longlat(pa_covid)

# Transform to NAD83 / Conus Albers
pa_covid <- st_transform(pa_covid, 5070)

# Verify the new CRS
st_crs(pa_covid)
st_is_longlat(pa_covid)
```

Answer:

1)  The Census boundaries arrive in NAD83, EPSG:4269. This is a
    geographic CRS, meaning locations are recorded as longitude and
    latitude in degrees.

2)  I transformed the county polygons to NAD83 / Conus Albers,
    EPSG:5070. This projection covers the contiguous United States,
    including all of Pennsylvania, so it avoids choosing just one State
    Plane or UTM zone. It preserves area and is suitable for a statewide
    county map.

3)  The projection affects the static maps and placement of proportional
    symbols. The joins, rates, SMRs, and Moran’s I do not depend on it
    when the county neighbour relationships stay the same. Leaflet
    requires a separate copy transformed to EPSG:4326.

## Part C --- Counts, rates, expected counts, and the SMR (4.5 points)

1.  Compute the **crude COVID-19 mortality rate per 100,000** for 2020
    in every county. Report the three highest and three lowest.
2.  Make two quick static maps with `ggplot2`, placed side by side: the
    **number of deaths** as **proportional symbols**, and the **crude
    rate** as a choropleth with a sequential, colour-blind-safe palette.
    Both need a legend title with units. In two or three sentences: why
    is a count shown with symbols rather than a choropleth, which
    counties stand out on each map, and why do the two maps tell
    different stories?
3.  Compute the **statewide reference rate**
    $r = \sum_i O_i / \sum_i P_i$, and from it the **expected count** in
    each county, $E_i = r \times P_i$. Show that
    $\sum_i E_i = \sum_i O_i$ and explain in one sentence why this must
    be so.
4.  Compute the **SMR**, $O_i / E_i$.
    a.  Interpret the SMR of one county of your choice in a full
        sentence a county commissioner could understand.
    b.  Divide each county's crude rate by the statewide rate and
        compare with the SMR. Explain why they are identical here, and
        what $E_i$ would have to take into account for the two to
        differ. *(This is where we are going later in the semester.)*
5.  Compute an exact **95% confidence interval** for every SMR (formula
    below). Compare the intervals for the two or three counties with the
    **fewest** deaths with those of the counties with the **highest**
    SMRs. In three or four sentences: what does this tell you about the
    extreme values on an SMR map?

::: callout-note
## Where the confidence interval comes from

Treat the expected count $E$ as a fixed constant and the observed count
as Poisson, $O \sim \text{Poisson}(\mu)$ with
$\mu = \text{SMR} \times E$. We first find an exact 95% interval for
$\mu$ and then divide both ends by $E$.

The lower bound $\mu_L$ is the value of $\mu$ at which observing $O$
**or more** deaths has probability 0.025; the upper bound $\mu_U$ is the
value at which observing $O$ **or fewer** has probability 0.025. Because
of the link between the Poisson and chi-square distributions, both have
a closed form:

$$\mu_L = \tfrac{1}{2}\,\chi^2_{0.025,\;2O}, \qquad
\mu_U = \tfrac{1}{2}\,\chi^2_{0.975,\;2(O+1)} .$$

Dividing by $E$ gives the interval for the SMR:

$$\left[\ \frac{\chi^2_{0.025,\,2O}}{2E}\ ,\ \ \frac{\chi^2_{0.975,\,2(O+1)}}{2E}\ \right].$$

The upper bound uses $2(O+1)$ degrees of freedom and the lower bound
$2O$; that asymmetry is what keeps the interval exact when counts are
small. When $O = 0$ the lower bound is 0.

**Worked example.** A county with $O = 4$ and $E = 5.57$ has SMR
$= 0.72$ and

``` r
qchisq(0.025, 2 * 4)       / (2 * 5.57)   # 0.20
qchisq(0.975, 2 * (4 + 1)) / (2 * 5.57)   # 1.84
poisson.test(4, T = 5.57)$conf.int        # same interval: E acts as the "time base"
```

The familiar normal approximation,
$\text{SMR} \times \exp(\pm 1.96/\sqrt{O})$, works for counties with
many deaths but breaks down for the smallest ones --- which are exactly
the counties this question is about --- and is undefined when $O = 0$.
:::

### Starting code

```{r}
#| label: c-starter

# C1 — deaths per 100,000 people
pa_covid <- pa_covid |>
  mutate(crude_rate = 100000 * deaths_2020 / Population)

# Three highest rates
pa_covid |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  arrange(desc(crude_rate)) |>
  select(NAME, deaths_2020, Population, crude_rate) |>
  head(3)

# Three lowest rates
pa_covid |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  arrange(crude_rate) |>
  select(NAME, deaths_2020, Population, crude_rate) |>
  head(3)

# C2 -- counts as proportional symbols
pts <- st_point_on_surface(pa_covid)        # one point inside each county

p_count <- ggplot() +
  geom_sf(
    data = pa_covid,
    fill = "grey95", colour = "grey70", linewidth = 0.15
  ) +
  geom_sf(
    data = pts, aes(size = deaths_2020),
    shape = 21, fill = "firebrick",
    colour = "white", alpha = 0.7
  ) +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 14, name = "Deaths (count)") +
  labs(title = "COVID-19 deaths, 2020") +
  theme_void()

# Rates as a choropleth
p_rate <- ggplot(pa_covid) +
  geom_sf(
    aes(fill = crude_rate),
    colour = "white", linewidth = 0.15
  ) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(
    option = "magma", direction = -1,
    name = "Deaths per\n100,000 people"
  ) +
  labs(title = "Crude mortality rate, 2020") +
  theme_void()

p_count + p_rate

# Identify counties that stand out on each map
pa_covid |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  arrange(desc(deaths_2020)) |>
  select(NAME, deaths_2020, crude_rate) |>
  head(3)

pa_covid |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  arrange(desc(crude_rate)) |>
  select(NAME, deaths_2020, crude_rate) |>
  head(3)

# C3 — statewide reference rate and expected deaths
r <- sum(pa_covid$deaths_2020) / sum(pa_covid$Population)

r * 100000

pa_covid <- pa_covid |>
  mutate(E = r * Population)

sum(pa_covid$E)
sum(pa_covid$deaths_2020)

# Check equality, allowing for tiny rounding differences
isTRUE(all.equal(
  sum(pa_covid$E),
  sum(pa_covid$deaths_2020)
))

# C4 — SMR and comparison with the rate ratio
pa_covid <- pa_covid |>
  mutate(
    SMR = deaths_2020 / E,
    rate_ratio = crude_rate / (r * 100000)
  )

isTRUE(all.equal(pa_covid$SMR, pa_covid$rate_ratio))

# Example county for interpretation
pa_covid |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  filter(NAME == "Lehigh") |>
  select(NAME, deaths_2020, E, SMR)


# C5 — exact 95% Poisson confidence intervals
pa_covid <- pa_covid |>
  mutate(
    SMR_lo = if_else(
      deaths_2020 == 0,
      0,
      qchisq(0.025, 2 * deaths_2020) / (2 * E)
    ),
    SMR_hi = qchisq(0.975, 2 * (deaths_2020 + 1)) / (2 * E)
  )

# Three counties with the fewest deaths
pa_covid |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  arrange(deaths_2020, NAME) |>
  select(NAME, deaths_2020, E, SMR, SMR_lo, SMR_hi) |>
  head(3)

# Three counties with the highest SMRs
pa_covid |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  arrange(desc(SMR)) |>
  select(NAME, deaths_2020, E, SMR, SMR_lo, SMR_hi) |>
  head(3)
```

Answer

1)  The three highest rates were Mifflin (257.92), Northumberland
    (248.78), and Bedford (196.29) deaths per 100,000 people. The three
    lowest were Wayne (35.05), Forest (41.396), and Greene (41.399)
    deaths per 100,000 people.

2)  Proportional symbols show death counts through circle area, so
    geographically large counties do not appear more important simply
    because of their size. Philadelphia, Montgomery, and Allegheny stand
    out for total deaths, while Mifflin, Northumberland, and Bedford
    have the highest crude rates. The maps tell different stories
    because counts show the total burden, while rates show deaths
    relative to population size.

3)  The statewide mortality rate was 125.21 deaths per 100,000 people.
    Both total expected and total observed deaths equal 16,030. They
    must be equal because the reference rate is total observed deaths
    divided by total population, and multiplying it by each county’s
    population and adding the results gives back the total observed
    deaths.

4)  

    a.  Lehigh County recorded 503 deaths, compared with about 462
        expected if it had the statewide mortality rate. Its SMR of
        1.088 means it recorded approximately 8.8% more deaths than
        expected.
    b.  The SMR and the county-to-state mortality rate ratio are
        identical here because expected deaths use only population size
        and the same statewide rate for every county. They could differ
        if expected deaths also accounted for population
        characteristics, such as age, using separate reference rates for
        different groups.

5)  The counties with only three or four deaths have much greater
    uncertainty relative to their SMR estimates. Sullivan’s and
    Cameron’s intervals include 1, so their results are compatible with
    the statewide rate, while Forest’s interval lies just below 1. The
    intervals for the three highest-SMR counties are all above 1,
    supporting higher mortality under the Poisson model. This shows why
    an extreme colour on an SMR map should be interpreted alongside the
    death count and confidence interval.

## Part D --- Mapping a ratio (3.5 points)

In Exercise 1 a sequential palette was the right choice for a rate. An
SMR is different: it is a ratio with a **meaningful reference value of
1**, and it is **multiplicative** --- an SMR of 2 is as far above
expected as 0.5 is below it.

1.  Map the SMR as an interactive **`leaflet`** map with a **diverging
    palette centred on 1** and **class breaks you set yourself**. Choose
    breaks that are symmetric on the ratio scale, and make the class
    around 1 read as "about as expected". Justify the palette and the
    breaks in three or four sentences.
2.  Your SMR map meets the standards from Exercise 1 --- legend title
    with units or meaning, thin boundaries, colour-blind-safe palette
    --- and in addition:
    - a **source line** on the map naming the data and the year;
    - a **popup** for each county giving the observed and expected
      deaths, the SMR, and its 95% interval from C5. This is what makes
      an interactive map worth having: the reader can check how much
      evidence stands behind a colour.

::: callout-warning
## `leaflet` wants longitude and latitude

Web maps are drawn on a Web Mercator basemap and expect coordinates in
**EPSG:4326**. Your `pa_covid` is now projected (Part B), so give
`leaflet` a transformed **copy**, `st_transform(pa_covid, 4326)`, and
keep the projected object for everything else. Handing it projected
coordinates is the most common reason for a blank `leaflet` map.
:::

::: callout-tip
## What earns full marks here

Breaks that follow from what an SMR *means*, not from the distribution
of the values. A student who can explain why 0.67 and 1.5 belong in the
same break set understands the variable.
:::

### Starting code

```{r}
#| label: d-starter

# Keep the projected object; make a longitude/latitude copy
pa_wgs <- st_transform(pa_covid, 4326)

# Reciprocal breaks, symmetric around 1 on the ratio scale
brks <- c(0, 1/2, 1/1.5, 1/1.1, 1.1, 1.5, 2, Inf)

pal <- colorBin(
  "RdBu",
  domain = pa_wgs$SMR,
  bins = brks,
  reverse = TRUE,
  right = FALSE
)

# One representative value per class for the legend
legend_values <- c(0.25, 0.60, 0.80, 1, 1.30, 1.75, 2.50)

legend_labels <- c(
  "< 0.50",
  "0.50 to < 0.67",
  "0.67 to < 0.91",
  "0.91 to < 1.10 (about as expected)",
  "1.10 to < 1.50",
  "1.50 to < 2.00",
  "2.00 or more"
)

leaflet(pa_wgs) |>
  addTiles() |>
  addPolygons(
    fillColor = ~pal(SMR),
    fillOpacity = 0.8,
    color = "white",
    weight = 0.6,
    label = ~NAME,
    popup = ~sprintf(
      paste0(
        "<b>%s County</b><br>",
        "Observed deaths: %d<br>",
        "Expected deaths: %.1f<br>",
        "SMR: %.2f<br>",
        "95%% confidence interval: %.2f–%.2f"
      ),
      NAME, deaths_2020, E, SMR, SMR_lo, SMR_hi
    ),
    highlightOptions = highlightOptions(
      weight = 2,
      color = "black",
      bringToFront = TRUE
    )
  ) |>
  addLegend(
    colors = pal(legend_values),
    labels = legend_labels,
    opacity = 0.8,
    title = "SMR: observed / expected deaths",
    position = "bottomright"
  ) |>
  addControl(
    paste0(
      "COVID-19 deaths: JHU CSSE, through Dec. 31, 2020",
      "<br>Population: Census 2019 estimates via JHU",
      "<br>Boundaries: U.S. Census Bureau, 2020",
      "<br>Legend boundaries rounded to two decimals"
    ),
    position = "bottomleft"
  )
```

Answer:

1)  I used a colour-blind-safe blue–white–red palette, with blue showing
    fewer deaths than expected and red showing more. The light central
    class, from approximately 0.91 to 1.10, is labelled “about as
    expected.” The breaks use reciprocal pairs, such as 0.5 and 2,
    because half the expected deaths and twice the expected deaths
    represent equal departures from 1 on the ratio scale. These breaks
    reflect what the SMR means rather than how the county values are
    distributed.

2)  The map has thin county boundaries and a legend titled “SMR:
    observed / expected deaths.” A source line identifies the JHU CSSE
    COVID-19 death data for 2020, the population estimates, and the
    county boundaries. Clicking a county opens a popup showing its
    observed deaths, expected deaths, SMR, and 95% confidence interval,
    allowing readers to check the uncertainty behind its colour.

::: callout-note
A `leaflet` map is an HTML widget: it appears in the rendered page on
your GitHub Pages site, which is where I grade it. It will not appear in
a PDF.
:::

## Part E --- Spatial weights and global Moran's I (4 points)

1.  Build a **queen contiguity** neighbour list. Report the average
    number of neighbours, the smallest and largest, and whether any
    county has none.
2.  Convert it to **row-standardized** spatial weights. One sentence:
    what does row standardization do to a county's neighbours, and what
    does the spatial lag of the SMR then represent?
3.  Compute **global Moran's I** for the SMR by permutation with
    `moran.mc()` (999 simulations; set a seed), and plot the permutation
    distribution with the observed value marked. Report $I$, its
    expectation under the null hypothesis, $-1/(n-1)$, and the
    $p$-value. In three or four sentences: what exactly is the null
    hypothesis, how does the simulation test it, and is there a spatial
    signal in the SMRs?
4.  Draw the **Moran scatterplot**, with every county labelled and
    coloured by quadrant. Name two or three counties in the high--high
    quadrant and two or three in the low--low quadrant, say in one
    sentence what the slope of the fitted line is, and say in one
    sentence what Moran's I does **not** tell you about these counties.

### Starting code

```{r}
#| label: e-starter
#| message: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 8

# E1 — queen contiguity neighbours
nb <- poly2nb(pa_covid, queen = TRUE)
summary(nb)

n_neighbours <- card(nb)

c(
  average = mean(n_neighbours),
  smallest = min(n_neighbours),
  largest = max(n_neighbours),
  counties_without_neighbours = sum(n_neighbours == 0)
)

# E2 — row-standardized weights
lw <- nb2listw(nb, style = "W")

# E3 — global Moran's I with 999 permutations
set.seed(374)
mc <- moran.mc(pa_covid$SMR, lw, nsim = 999)
mc

c(
  observed_I = unname(mc$statistic),
  expected_I = -1 / (nrow(pa_covid) - 1),
  p_value = mc$p.value
)

# mc$res includes the observed I as its last element;
# exclude it when plotting the 999 shuffled results
simulated_I <- head(mc$res, -1)

hist(
  simulated_I,
  breaks = 40,
  main = "Permutation distribution of Moran's I",
  xlab = "Moran's I",
  col = "grey80",
  border = "white"
)

abline(v = mc$statistic, col = "red", lwd = 2)
abline(
  v = -1 / (nrow(pa_covid) - 1),
  col = "black", lty = 2
)

legend(
  "topright",
  legend = c("Observed I", "Null expectation"),
  col = c("red", "black"),
  lty = c(1, 2),
  lwd = c(2, 1),
  bty = "n"
)

# E4 — spatial lag and scatterplot quadrants
mp_df <- pa_covid |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  mutate(
    lag_SMR = lag.listw(lw, SMR),
    quad = case_when(
      SMR >= mean(SMR) & lag_SMR >= mean(SMR) ~ "High-High",
      SMR < mean(SMR) & lag_SMR < mean(SMR) ~ "Low-Low",
      SMR >= mean(SMR) & lag_SMR < mean(SMR) ~ "High-Low",
      TRUE ~ "Low-High"
    )
  )

ggplot(mp_df, aes(SMR, lag_SMR)) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = mean(mp_df$SMR),
    linetype = 2, colour = "grey60"
  ) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = mean(mp_df$SMR),
    linetype = 2, colour = "grey60"
  ) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "lm", se = FALSE,
    colour = "black", linewidth = 0.5
  ) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = quad), size = 2) +
  geom_text_repel(
    aes(label = NAME),
    size = 2.6, max.overlaps = Inf,
    seed = 374
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c(
      "High-High" = "#D55E00",
      "Low-Low" = "#0072B2",
      "High-Low" = "#CC79A7",
      "Low-High" = "#009E73"
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "County SMR (observed / expected deaths)",
    y = "Mean SMR of neighbouring counties",
    colour = NULL,
    title = "Moran scatterplot: Pennsylvania, 2020"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

table(mp_df$quad)

# Show three examples from each requested quadrant
mp_df |>
  filter(quad == "High-High") |>
  arrange(desc(SMR)) |>
  select(NAME, SMR, lag_SMR, quad) |>
  head(3)

mp_df |>
  filter(quad == "Low-Low") |>
  arrange(SMR) |>
  select(NAME, SMR, lag_SMR, quad) |>
  head(3)

# Check that the fitted slope equals Moran's I
c(
  slope = unname(coef(lm(lag_SMR ~ SMR, data = mp_df))[2]),
  Moran_I = unname(mc$statistic)
)
```

Answer:

1)  Counties were treated as neighbours if they shared a boundary or a
    corner. The average number of neighbours was 5.10, the smallest was
    2, and the largest was 9. No county had zero neighbours.

2)  Row standardization gives each county’s neighbours equal weights
    that add up to 1, so the spatial lag represents the average SMR of
    its neighbouring counties.

3)  The observed Moran’s I was 0.2893, compared with a null expectation
    of −0.01515, with a permutation p-value of 0.001. The null
    hypothesis is that the SMRs are randomly arranged across the
    counties, with no spatial association under the chosen neighbour
    relationships. The test shuffled the SMRs across the counties 999
    times and compared the resulting Moran’s I values with the observed
    value. The positive I and small p-value provide strong evidence that
    counties with similar SMRs tend to be neighbours.

4)  Mifflin, Northumberland, and Bedford are examples in the high–high
    quadrant, while Wayne, Forest, and Greene are examples in the
    low–low quadrant. The fitted line’s slope is 0.2893, equal to global
    Moran’s I with these row-standardized weights. Global Moran’s I
    describes the overall spatial pattern but does not establish whether
    any individual county belongs to a statistically significant local
    cluster.
